Jobs lost to AI, consent, union contracts and the laws protecting voice actors in the US and Canada. Every figure is named, dated and linked to its source.

About **1 in 5 US voice actors** (21%) say they have knowingly lost a job to an AI voice, according to the National Association of Voice Actors’ 2026 survey. Only **13%** have agreed to let anyone build a synthetic version of their voice, yet 9% know of one made without their permission. This page collects the numbers on AI and voice actors in the US and Canada: jobs, consent, union contracts, laws and the market. Every figure is named, dated and linked to its source.

## AI and Voice Actor Stats (Top Picks)

- **21%** of voice actors say they have knowingly lost a job to a synthetic voice (NAVA, 2026).
- **9%** know of a synthetic version of their voice, or a character they voiced, made without permission (NAVA, 2026).
- **53%** would be open to an ethically created synthetic version of their voice in future (NAVA, 2026).
- **95.04%** of SAG-AFTRA members voted to approve the 2025 video game agreement, which requires consent and disclosure for AI digital replicas (SAG-AFTRA, 2025).
- AI-narrated audiobooks made just **0.03%** of audiobook sales revenue tracked by the Audio Publishers Association in 2025 (Audio Publishers Association, 2026).
- **98%** of Canadian performers surveyed by ACTRA named misuse of their name, image and likeness as a concern (ACTRA via Playback, 2023).

## What this means for teams building AI voices

The numbers point one way. Most voice actors have not consented to synthesis, but over half would consider it on ethical terms. Contracts and state laws in the US increasingly require written consent and a clear description of use. A voice model trained on recordings without that paperwork is now a legal and reputational risk.

Flaunt Audio records TTS training data and custom AI voices with contracted, paid voice actors, with consent documented for every speaker. See our approach to compliance and ethics.

## AI and Voice Actors FAQ

### How many voice actors have lost work to AI?

21% of voice actors say they have knowingly lost a job to a synthetic voice, according to NAVA’s 2026 survey of 1,379 respondents.

### Do voice actors consent to AI voice cloning?

Most have not. 13% have agreed to let a third party create a synthetic version of their voice, while 53% say they would be open to an ethically created one in future (NAVA, 2026).

### Is AI voice cloning legal in the US?

It depends on the state and on consent. Tennessee’s ELVIS Act and California’s AB 2602 and AB 1836 restrict unauthorised digital replicas. The federal NO FAKES Act has been introduced but is not yet law.

### Are Canadian voice actors protected from AI cloning?

Canada has no specific federal law protecting a person’s voice. Performers rely on common law and a few provincial privacy acts, and on union agreements negotiated by ACTRA.

## How many voice actors are there in the US and Canada?

Nobody counts voice actors on their own. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics groups them with all actors, and Statistics Canada does the same. These are the closest reliable figures:

- US employers held **67,500** actor jobs in 2025, including voice-over and narration work. Median pay was**$29.05 an hour** (May 2025) (US BLS).
- The BLS projects **0% job growth** for actors from 2025 to 2035, with about**6,300 openings a year** from people leaving the field (US BLS).
- SAG-AFTRA, the main US performers’ union, represents approximately **160,000** members, voice-over talent among them (SAG-AFTRA).
- ACTRA sent its AI survey to more than **28,000** members across Canada (Playback).

## How many voice actors have lost work to AI?

The best data comes from the National Association of Voice Actors’ State of Voiceover Survey 2026: 1,379 responses collected between 22 January and 22 February 2026.

- **21%** of voice actors say they have knowingly lost a job to a synthetic voice (NAVA, 2026).
- **11%** know of a synthetic version of their voice being used in a professional project (NAVA, 2026).
- In Canada, **93%** of performers surveyed by ACTRA expect AI to eventually replace human actors in certain roles. The survey closed in December 2023 and ACTRA did not publish the number of respondents (ACTRA via Playback).

## How many voice actors have consented to AI cloning?

- Only **13%** of voice actors have agreed to let a third party create a synthetic version of their voice.**87%** have not (NAVA, 2026).
- **9%** know of a synthetic version of their voice, or of a character they voiced, created without their permission (NAVA, 2026).
- **53%** would be open to an ethically created synthetic version of their voice in future.**47%** would not (NAVA, 2026).
- **27%** of people buying AI voices do not check a provider’s ethical AI stance (Voices 2025 Audio Trends Report).

## What do union contracts say about AI voices?

- SAG-AFTRA members approved the 2025 Video Game (Interactive Media) Agreement by **95.04% to 4.96%** on 9 July 2025, ending a strike of about 11 months. The deal requires consent and disclosure for AI digital replicas and lets performers suspend consent to new AI material during a strike (SAG-AFTRA).
- The same agreement includes a **15.17%** compounded pay rise on ratification, then 3% each November from 2025 to 2027 (SAG-AFTRA).
- SAG-AFTRA’s 2025 Commercials Contracts passed with **96.90%** support, adding informed consent and compensation guardrails for AI and**$218.4 million** in new earnings and benefit contributions over three years (SAG-AFTRA).

## Which laws protect voice actors from AI cloning?

- **Tennessee’s** ELVIS Act, signed on 21 March 2024, added voice to the state’s protections for a person’s name, image and likeness (Tennessee Governor’s Office). It took effect on 1 July 2024.
- **California** signed AB 2602 and AB 1836 on 17 September 2024. AB 2602 requires contracts to describe how a performer’s AI digital replica will be used. AB 1836 requires estate consent for digital replicas of deceased performers (Governor of California).
- A revised federal **NO FAKES Act** was introduced on 20 May 2026 with the backing of 37 organisations. It would make distributing an unauthorised digital replica of a person’s voice or likeness illegal. It is not yet law (Office of Sen. Marsha Blackburn).
- **Canada** has no federal law giving people a specific right over their voice. The Artificial Intelligence and Data Act (part of Bill C-27) stalled in Parliament, and performers rely on the common law tort of misappropriation of personality and a few provincial privacy acts (OpenMedia, 2026).

## How fast is the AI voice market growing?

- ElevenLabs raised **$500 million at an $11 billion valuation** in February 2026 and reported over**$330 million** in annual recurring revenue at the end of 2025 (ElevenLabs).
- Voice creators have earned over **$22 million** from ElevenLabs’ Voice Library, across 10,400+ creators in 32 languages (ElevenLabs, 2026).
- Audiobook sales tracked by the US-based Audio Publishers Association reached **$2.43 billion** in 2025, up 9%. AI-narrated titles made**0.03%** of that revenue. Only 16% of listeners have heard an AI-voiced audiobook, and willingness to try one fell from 70% in 2025 to 61% in 2026 (Audio Publishers Association, 2026).
- YouTube’s AI auto-dubbing covers **27 languages** , with over 6 million daily viewers watching at least 10 minutes of dubbed content in December 2025 (Google, 2026).
- One research firm values the AI voice generator market at **$4.16 billion** in 2025, rising to $20.71 billion by 2031. Market-size estimates vary widely between firms (MarketsandMarkets).

## Key lawsuits over AI voices

- **Lehrman and Sage v. Lovo** (S.D.N.Y.): two voice actors paid $1,200 and $400 through Fiverr for recordings described as internal research sued over AI clones of their voices. On 10 July 2025 the court let their breach of contract, New York right of publicity and consumer protection claims proceed, and dismissed the trademark claims and copyright claims over the AI clones (US District Court, S.D.N.Y.).
- **OpenAI’s “Sky” voice** was paused on 19 May 2024. OpenAI said its five ChatGPT voices were chosen from more than 400 submissions from voice and screen actors (OpenAI).
